description: The Adobe Firefly-powered generative commands introduced through Photoshop 2025 (v26) - Generative Fill, Generative Expand, Generate Image, Generate Background, Generative Remove and their supporting controls - together with the docked panels that carry day-to-day editing state and the workspace, companion-app and output features that surround them. Generative features run on Adobe's servers, require an internet connection, and consume generative credits from the signed-in Creative Cloud plan.

tools.name: Generative Fill
tools.description: Replaces or fills an active selection with Adobe Firefly-generated content that is matched to the perspective, lighting and colour of the surrounding pixels. Type a short prompt to add something to the selection, or leave the prompt empty so Photoshop removes what is there and rebuilds the background from context. The result is written to a new Generative Layer that carries its own layer mask, so the original pixels are never altered and the prompt can be changed later. Use it for adding or removing objects, swapping clothing and products, and extending sets or skies.
tools.usage: Make a selection with any selection tool, then Edit > Generative Fill..., or click Generative Fill in the Contextual Task Bar that appears beneath the selection. There is no default keyboard shortcut. The prompt field, Generate button and model picker live in the Contextual Task Bar; the returned variations live in Window > Properties.

parameters.name: Prompt
parameters.description: Short English description of what should appear in the selection. Leave it blank for a context-aware fill, which is how you remove an object.

parameters.name: Reference Image
parameters.description: Optional image loaded from the icon at the right of the prompt field; it guides the style or content of the variations.

parameters.name: Generate
parameters.description: Sends the selection and prompt to Adobe Firefly and returns three variations per click. Clicking Generate again adds three more without discarding the earlier ones.

parameters.name: Variations (Properties panel)
parameters.description: Thumbnails of every generated result. Click one to swap it onto the canvas.

parameters.name: Enhance Detail
parameters.description: Button in the Properties panel that re-renders the chosen variation at higher resolution; available when the generated region is larger than about 1024 pixels.

tools.example:
1. Open the image and choose the Lasso tool (L).
2. Draw a rough selection around the area to change, overlapping the surrounding pixels slightly.
3. Click Generative Fill in the Contextual Task Bar.
4. Type a short prompt such as 'camping tent' - or leave it empty to delete the object - and click Generate.
5. Open Window > Properties and click through the three variation thumbnails to pick the best one.
6. Click Generate again in the Properties panel for three more variations, or click Enhance Detail to re-render the chosen one at higher quality.
tools.notes: Every Generate click spends generative credits. Short, concrete prompts work better than long sentences. The Generative Layer is non-destructive: you can edit its mask, change the prompt, or delete it entirely. Firefly generation needs an internet connection and is subject to Adobe's content guidelines, so some prompts are refused.

tools.name: Generative Expand
tools.description: Enlarges the canvas with the Crop tool and fills the newly exposed area with Firefly-generated content that continues the existing scene. It is the fastest way to change an image's aspect ratio - for example turning a 4:3 photograph into a 16:9 banner - without losing any of the original frame. A prompt is optional: leave it empty and Photoshop simply extends what is already there, or supply one to add specific content in the new space. Like Generative Fill, the result lands on a Generative Layer with three selectable variations.
tools.usage: Select the Crop tool (C), set Fill: Generative Expand in the options bar, drag a crop handle (or set a ratio) beyond the existing canvas, then type an optional prompt and click Generate in the Contextual Task Bar.

parameters.name: Fill (Crop tool options bar)
parameters.description: Dropdown that must be set to Generative Expand; the other choices are Background and Content-Aware, which do not use Firefly.

parameters.name: Ratio / W x H
parameters.description: Crop tool options-bar preset that sets the target aspect ratio before you drag the handles.

parameters.name: Prompt
parameters.description: Optional description of what to put in the new area. Leave blank to extend the existing scene.

parameters.name: Generate
parameters.description: Runs the expansion and returns three variations in the Properties panel.

tools.example:
1. Press C for the Crop tool.
2. In the options bar set Fill: Generative Expand.
3. Choose a Ratio such as 16:9, or drag the side handles outward past the image edge.
4. Leave the Contextual Task Bar prompt empty to extend the scene, or type something like 'sandy beach'.
5. Click Generate.
6. Pick the best of the three variations in Window > Properties.
tools.notes: If the Generate button never appears, the Crop tool's Fill dropdown is still on Background - this is the most common cause of a missing Generative Expand bar. Expanding one side at a time gives you independent variation choices per side. Each generation costs generative credits.

tools.name: Generate Image
tools.description: Creates a complete image from a text prompt on an empty document or transparent layer, rather than filling part of an existing photograph. Photoshop shows the prompt field in the Contextual Task Bar, optionally accepts a reference image and style settings, and returns three variations on a Generative Layer. Use it to rough out a concept, build a backdrop from scratch, or produce placeholder art inside an existing composition.
tools.usage: Create a new document (File > New, Ctrl+N) or add an empty/transparent layer, then click Generate Image in the Contextual Task Bar, enter a prompt, optionally add a reference image or style settings, and click Generate. The Contextual Task Bar shows Generate Image only while the active layer is empty or transparent.

parameters.name: Prompt
parameters.description: Text description of the image to create.

parameters.name: Model picker
parameters.description: Chooses which Adobe Firefly image model generates the result; the available models change with the Photoshop version and plan.

parameters.name: Reference Image
parameters.description: Optional source image that steers composition or style.

parameters.name: Style settings
parameters.description: Optional effects, colour and lighting presets applied to the generation.

parameters.name: Generate
parameters.description: Produces three variations, shown in the Contextual Task Bar and the Properties panel.

tools.example:
1. File > New (Ctrl+N), pick a size, click Create.
2. In the Contextual Task Bar click Generate Image.
3. Type a prompt such as 'misty pine forest at dawn'.
4. Optionally open the model picker and the style settings to steer the look.
5. Click Generate and choose a variation in Window > Properties.
tools.notes: The Contextual Task Bar is context sensitive: an empty layer offers Generate Image, while a partial selection on an existing image offers Generative Fill instead. Generated images are written to a Generative Layer, so the document can still be built up in layers afterwards. Costs generative credits per click.

tools.name: Generate Background
tools.description: Replaces the background behind a cut-out subject with a Firefly-generated scene that is matched to the subject's lighting, shadows and perspective. It is a two-step workflow: remove the background first, then describe the replacement. This is the quickest route to product shots and portraits on a new setting without manual compositing. As with the other generative commands you get three variations to choose from.
tools.usage: Select a standard pixel layer, click Remove background in the Contextual Task Bar (or Window > Properties > Quick Actions > Remove Background), then click Generate Background in the Contextual Task Bar, type a prompt and click Generate.

parameters.name: Prompt
parameters.description: Description of the background to create, for example 'rooftop, city skyline at dusk'.

parameters.name: Generate
parameters.description: Runs the generation; one standard generative credit is deducted per generation.

parameters.name: Variations
parameters.description: Alternative backgrounds shown in the Contextual Task Bar and the Properties panel.

tools.example:
1. Open the portrait or product shot and unlock the Background layer by double-clicking it.
2. Click Remove background in the Contextual Task Bar.
3. Click Generate Background.
4. Type 'rooftop, big city skyscrapers' and click Generate.
5. Cycle through the variations and keep the one that matches the subject's light direction.
tools.notes: Keeping part of the original background - for example the floor the subject stands on - gives far more believable results: make a rectangular selection over the area you want to keep before generating. Generate Similar can then be used on the variation you like best to refine it further.

tools.name: Generative Remove (Remove tool with Generative AI)
tools.description: The generative object-removal workflow: brush over an unwanted object with the Remove tool and Adobe Firefly rebuilds the area with entirely new content instead of cloning nearby pixels. Turning on the Generative AI option in the options bar sends the brushed area to Adobe's servers, which handles complex backgrounds that the local content-aware engine smears. The same tool's Find Distractions menu offers one-click removal of wires and cables or of distracting people across the whole frame. Use it for power lines, tourists, signage, blemishes and any object whose background is too busy for Content-Aware Fill.
tools.usage: Remove tool (J - it shares the Spot Healing Brush group in the toolbar), then turn on Generative AI in the options bar and brush over the object; release the mouse to run the removal. Find Distractions in the same options bar gives the Wires and Cables and People one-click options. An equivalent route is to select the object and click Generate with an empty prompt in the Generative Fill field of the Contextual Task Bar; the classic non-generative alternatives are Edit > Content-Aware Fill... and Edit > Fill (Shift+F5) > Content-Aware.

parameters.name: Generative AI
parameters.description: Options-bar switch that routes the removal through Adobe Firefly instead of the on-device engine. Leave it off (Auto) for small, simple blemishes where speed matters.

parameters.name: Find Distractions
parameters.description: Options-bar menu with Wires and Cables and People - Photoshop finds and removes them across the image in one click.

parameters.name: Size
parameters.description: Brush diameter; [ and ] change it while you paint.

parameters.name: Remove after each stroke
parameters.description: Options-bar toggle that runs the fill as soon as you release the mouse, rather than waiting for you to confirm.

tools.example:
1. Press J until the Remove tool is active.
2. In the options bar turn on Generative AI.
3. Set a brush size slightly larger than the object and paint over it, including its shadow.
4. Release the mouse and wait for the progress bar - Photoshop is calling the Firefly service.
5. For power lines instead, open Find Distractions in the options bar and choose Wires and Cables.
tools.notes: Generative removal needs an internet connection and spends generative credits; the Auto (non-generative) mode is free and instant but weaker on busy backgrounds. Always brush the object's shadow and reflection as well, or they survive the removal. Work on a duplicate layer if you want to keep the untouched original.

tools.name: Reference Image (in Generative Fill)
tools.description: Loads a second image that steers what Generative Fill produces, giving far more control than a text prompt alone. It is the practical way to match a specific garment, product, texture or art style that is difficult to describe in words. The reference is combined with the selection and any prompt text, and still returns three variations. It also works with Generate Image, Generative Expand and Generate Background.
tools.usage: Make a selection > Generative Fill in the Contextual Task Bar > click the Reference Image (small image) icon at the right of the prompt field > choose an image file > optionally type a prompt > Generate.

parameters.name: Reference Image icon
parameters.description: Appears in the Generative Fill prompt field of the Contextual Task Bar once the insertion point is in that field.

parameters.name: Reference image file
parameters.description: The image whose style, object or composition should guide the generation.

parameters.name: Prompt
parameters.description: Optional text used together with the reference to describe the result.

tools.example:
1. Use the Object Selection tool (W) to select the garment you want to replace.
2. Click Generative Fill in the Contextual Task Bar.
3. Click the Reference Image icon and open a photograph of the replacement garment.
4. Type a short prompt such as 'grey hoodie' to reinforce the reference, then click Generate.
5. Choose a variation in Window > Properties and click Enhance Detail if the result is soft.
tools.notes: If the Reference Image icon does not appear, click inside the Generative Fill prompt field first - the icon is only drawn once the field has focus. Keep the reference tightly cropped on the thing you want copied; busy references dilute the result.

tools.name: Generate Similar
tools.description: Takes one generated variation you already like and produces new variations close to it, instead of rolling the dice again from the prompt alone. Added in Photoshop 2025 (v26), it turns generative work from random re-rolling into directed iteration. It is available from the ellipsis menu on any variation thumbnail and works with the Generative Fill, Generative Expand, Generate Background and Generate Image workflows.
tools.usage: After any generation, open Window > Properties, switch to the Variations tab, hover over the variation you want to build on, click its ellipsis (...) menu and choose Generate Similar. The same command is available from the More actions (...) menu on a variation in the Contextual Task Bar.

parameters.name: Source variation
parameters.description: The generated result that the new variations are based on. Pick the one closest to your goal before running the command.

parameters.name: Generate Similar
parameters.description: Menu item on the variation's ellipsis menu; each run returns new comparable variations and updates the canvas.

tools.example:
1. Run Generative Fill with a prompt such as 'camping tent' and click Generate.
2. Open Window > Properties and go to the Variations tab.
3. Find the variation that is closest to what you want.
4. Click the ellipsis (...) on that thumbnail and choose Generate Similar.
5. Repeat on the new results until the composition is right.
tools.notes: Verified feature - it is documented by Adobe as Generate Similar and was introduced in the Photoshop 2025 release. Each Generate Similar run is a fresh generation and therefore spends generative credits like any other.

tools.name: Remove Background
tools.description: One-click subject isolation: Photoshop finds the main subject and hides everything else behind a layer mask, leaving a transparent background. Unlike the generative features it runs on Adobe Sensei, not Firefly, so it is instant and does not spend generative credits. It is the normal first step before Generate Background, before placing a subject on a new layout, or before exporting a transparent PNG. The related Select > Subject command produces the same selection without creating the mask.
tools.usage: Window > Properties > Quick Actions > Remove Background with a standard (unlocked) pixel layer selected, or click Remove background in the Contextual Task Bar. No default keyboard shortcut. Related: Select > Subject; Select > Select and Mask... (Alt+Ctrl+R) to refine the result.

parameters.name: Remove Background (Quick Actions)
parameters.description: Button in the Properties panel; requires a standard pixel layer - it is greyed out or missing for a locked Background layer, a Smart Object or an adjustment layer.

parameters.name: Select Subject and Remove Background processing
parameters.description: Edit > Preferences > Image Processing lets you choose Device (quicker) or Cloud (often more accurate) processing for both commands.

parameters.name: Layer mask
parameters.description: The result is a mask, not deleted pixels, so it can be painted on with a brush or refined in Select and Mask.

tools.example:
1. Double-click the locked Background layer in the Layers panel and click OK to convert it to a normal layer.
2. Open Window > Properties.
3. Under Quick Actions click Remove Background.
4. Inspect the edge; click the mask thumbnail and paint with a soft black or white brush to fix any misses.
5. Optionally press Alt+Ctrl+R for Select and Mask to refine hair with Refine Edge Brush.
tools.notes: If Remove Background is missing from the Properties panel, the selected layer is not a standard pixel layer - unlock the Background layer first. Hair and fine transparency almost always need a pass through Select and Mask; the one-click result is a starting point, not a finished cut-out.

tools.name: Contextual Task Bar
tools.description: A floating on-canvas bar that shows the most likely next actions for whatever you are doing - Select Subject and Remove Background on a plain layer, Generative Fill on a partial selection, Generate Image on an empty layer, crop and transform controls during those operations. It is the primary entry point for every generative feature, because the prompt field, model picker, Reference Image icon and Generate button all live in it. Drag its left handle to reposition it, or hide it when it covers your work.
tools.usage: Window > Contextual Task Bar toggles it on and off. No default keyboard shortcut; Ctrl+F opens the Discover search box, where typing 'Contextual Task Bar' also toggles it. Drag the handle at the left edge to move it; its ellipsis (...) menu offers Reset bar position, Pin bar position and Hide bar.

parameters.name: Window > Contextual Task Bar
parameters.description: Checkbox menu item that shows or hides the bar.

parameters.name: Ellipsis (...) menu
parameters.description: Reset bar position, Pin bar position, Hide bar.

parameters.name: Context
parameters.description: The buttons change with the active tool, layer and selection - empty layer gives Generate Image, partial selection gives Generative Fill, plain pixel layer gives Select Subject and Remove Background.

tools.example:
1. Open Window and make sure Contextual Task Bar is ticked.
2. Select a pixel layer in the Layers panel - the bar stays hidden if no usable layer is active.
3. Draw a selection; the bar switches to show Generative Fill.
4. Drag the bar by its left handle away from the area you are editing.
5. Use the ellipsis menu > Pin bar position to stop it following your selection.
tools.notes: The most common complaint is that the bar does not appear: it needs both the Window menu item ticked and a suitable layer selected. Some workflows - Crop, Place, Free Transform - keep the bar visible regardless, because it carries the Cancel and Done controls for those operations.

tools.name: Adobe Firefly integration & generative credits
tools.description: Every generative command in Photoshop - Generative Fill, Generative Expand, Generate Image, Generate Background, Generate Similar and the Remove tool's Generative AI mode - calls an Adobe Firefly model running on Adobe's servers and spends generative credits from the signed-in Creative Cloud plan. Firefly models are trained on licensed Adobe Stock and public-domain content, which is why Adobe positions the output as safe for commercial use. Photoshop 2025 adds a model picker in the Contextual Task Bar so you can choose which Firefly model generates a result. Knowing your credit balance matters because generations stop being fast (or stop entirely) once monthly credits run out.
tools.usage: Credits are consumed automatically by each Generate click; there is no separate command. Check the balance from the Account menu in Photoshop, from the avatar at the top right of the Creative Cloud desktop app or Adobe account page, or at firefly.adobe.com. The model picker sits in the Contextual Task Bar next to the prompt field. A signed-in Adobe ID and an internet connection are required.

parameters.name: Generative credits
parameters.description: Monthly allowance included with a Creative Cloud plan; one standard credit is deducted per generation for the image features. The allowance differs sharply between plans and has changed over time, so check your own plan rather than assuming a number.

parameters.name: Model picker
parameters.description: Contextual Task Bar dropdown that selects the Firefly model used for the current generation; the list of available models changes with the Photoshop version and the plan.

parameters.name: Account menu
parameters.description: In-app place to view how many generative credits the plan includes and how many have been used.

parameters.name: Content Credentials
parameters.description: Generated content carries Adobe's Content Credentials metadata identifying it as AI-generated.

tools.example:
1. Sign in to Photoshop with the Adobe ID that holds the Creative Cloud plan.
2. Open the Account menu in Photoshop to see the plan's generative credit allowance and usage.
3. Before a large batch of generations, check the remaining balance - each Generate click, including Generate Similar, costs credits.
4. When running Generative Fill, open the model picker in the Contextual Task Bar and choose the Firefly model that suits the job.
5. If generations fail, confirm the internet connection and that the prompt does not breach Adobe's content guidelines.
tools.notes: Credit allowances and plan tiers change regularly - treat any specific number you read as version- and date-dependent and verify it on Adobe's generative credits help page. Generation is a network round trip, so results are slower than local filters and unavailable offline. Prompts are moderated server-side and some are refused.

tools.name: Properties
tools.description: The context-sensitive panel that shows the settings for whatever is currently selected: document size and resolution when nothing is selected, Quick Actions such as Remove Background and Select Subject on a pixel layer, the controls for an adjustment layer, the feather and density of a mask, type and shape attributes, and the variations returned by any generative command. It has largely replaced the individual Masks and Type option dialogs. Because it carries the generative Variations tab and the Enhance Detail button, it is a permanent fixture of any Photoshop 2025 generative workflow.
tools.usage: Window > Properties. No default keyboard shortcut. Docked on the right in the Essentials workspace; double-clicking an adjustment layer thumbnail or a layer mask also brings it forward.

parameters.name: Quick Actions
parameters.description: Remove Background and Select Subject buttons shown for a standard pixel layer.

parameters.name: Variations tab
parameters.description: Thumbnails of generated results, with the ellipsis menu that carries Generate Similar, plus the Enhance Detail button.

parameters.name: Adjustment controls
parameters.description: Curves, Levels, Hue/Saturation and the other adjustment-layer interfaces appear here rather than in a dialog.

parameters.name: Masks
parameters.description: Density, Feather, Select and Mask, Colour Range and Invert for the selected layer or vector mask.

tools.example:
1. Window > Properties to open the panel.
2. Click a plain pixel layer - the panel shows document info and Quick Actions.
3. Click the layer mask thumbnail - the panel switches to Density and Feather sliders.
4. Run Generative Fill - the panel switches to the Variations tab.
5. Click a variation thumbnail's ellipsis and choose Generate Similar to iterate.

tools.name: Adjustments
tools.description: A grid of icons that create adjustment layers - Brightness/Contrast, Levels, Curves, Exposure, Vibrance, Hue/Saturation, Colour Balance, Black & White, Photo Filter, Channel Mixer, Colour Lookup, Invert, Posterize, Threshold, Gradient Map and Selective Colour - in one click. Because they are layers, the underlying pixels are untouched and the settings stay editable, which is why this panel should be used in preference to the destructive commands under Image > Adjustments. Photoshop 2025 also surfaces one-click Adjustment Presets at the top of the panel. The actual controls for whichever adjustment you create appear in the Properties panel.
tools.usage: Window > Adjustments. No default keyboard shortcut. The same adjustment layers can be created from Layer > New Adjustment Layer > ... or from the half-filled circle icon at the bottom of the Layers panel.

parameters.name: Adjustment Presets
parameters.description: Grouped one-click looks (portrait, landscape, cinematic, black and white and so on) that drop in a stack of adjustment layers.

parameters.name: Adjustment icons
parameters.description: Each icon creates the corresponding adjustment layer directly above the active layer, with a white (fully revealing) mask.

parameters.name: Clip to layer
parameters.description: Alt+click the boundary between the adjustment layer and the layer below, or use the clip icon in Properties, to limit the adjustment to one layer.

tools.example:
1. Window > Adjustments.
2. Click the Curves icon - a Curves adjustment layer appears above the active layer.
3. Shape the curve in Window > Properties.
4. Alt+click the line between the adjustment layer and the layer below to clip it to that layer only.
5. Paint black on the adjustment layer's mask to hide the effect locally.

tools.name: Channels
tools.description: Lists the colour channels of the document (composite plus Red/Green/Blue, or Cyan/Magenta/Yellow/Black in CMYK), any spot colour channels, and any alpha channels holding saved selections. Viewing a single channel is the standard way to find the highest-contrast starting point for a luminosity mask or a hair selection. Alpha channels let you store a selection in the file and reload it later with Ctrl+click on the channel thumbnail.
tools.usage: Window > Channels. No default keyboard shortcut. Ctrl+click a channel thumbnail loads it as a selection; Select > Save Selection writes a new alpha channel.

parameters.name: Composite channel
parameters.description: Top entry (RGB, CMYK or Lab); click it to return to normal colour viewing.

parameters.name: Alpha channel
parameters.description: Greyscale stored selection. Preserved only in PSD, PSB, PDF, TIFF and raw formats.

parameters.name: Spot channel
parameters.description: Extra ink channel for print work, added from the panel menu > New Spot Channel.

parameters.name: Load channel as selection
parameters.description: Ctrl+click the thumbnail, or the dotted-circle icon at the bottom of the panel.

tools.notes: Saving to a format that does not support alpha channels (JPEG, most PNG workflows) silently discards them. Turning channel thumbnails off in Panel Options speeds up very large documents.

tools.name: Paths
tools.description: Lists every saved path in the document plus the temporary Work Path and the vector mask of a selected shape layer. Paths drawn with the Pen tool (P) or converted from a selection give you resolution-independent, perfectly smooth outlines that can be converted back to a selection, stroked with any brush, or used as a clipping path for print. Use it whenever an edge is geometric or a selection must survive scaling.
tools.usage: Window > Paths. No default keyboard shortcut. Ctrl+click a path thumbnail to load it as a selection; the icons along the bottom of the panel fill the path, stroke it with the current brush, make a selection from it, make a work path from a selection, add a mask, and create a new path.

parameters.name: Work Path
parameters.description: Temporary path created by the Pen tool or Make Work Path; it is replaced the next time you draw, so double-click and name it to keep it.

parameters.name: Make selection
parameters.description: Converts the path to a selection with an optional feather radius.

parameters.name: Stroke path with brush
parameters.description: Paints the current brush along the path - the basis of clean freehand-looking strokes.

parameters.name: Clipping path
parameters.description: Panel menu > Clipping Path... marks a saved path as the print clipping path for placement in InDesign or a RIP.

tools.notes: Work paths are volatile - always double-click and rename a work path before drawing the next one. You cannot reorder vector masks or work paths in the panel, only saved paths.

tools.name: History
tools.description: Records every edit made in the current session as a separate state and lets you jump back to any of them, which is a much faster form of undo than repeated Ctrl+Z. Snapshots taken from the panel are permanent markers that survive as older states fall off the end of the list. The History Brush (Y) paints selectively from a chosen state or snapshot, so you can undo one part of a change without undoing the rest. History is session-only: closing the document discards it.
tools.usage: Window > History. No default keyboard shortcut. Ctrl+Z steps back one state, Ctrl+Alt+Z steps backwards repeatedly, Ctrl+Shift+Z steps forward. The number of states kept is set in Edit > Preferences > Performance > History & Cache > History States.

parameters.name: History States
parameters.description: Preferences > Performance setting for how many states are kept (default 50). Higher values use more scratch disk.

parameters.name: Snapshot
parameters.description: Camera icon at the bottom of the panel; a named, permanent copy of the current state for this session.

parameters.name: New document from current state
parameters.description: Leftmost icon at the bottom; creates a new document from the selected history state.

parameters.name: Set source for history brush
parameters.description: Click the box to the left of a state, then paint with the History Brush (Y) to restore that state locally.

tools.example:
1. Window > History.
2. Before a risky edit, click the camera icon to take a snapshot and rename it 'before retouch'.
3. Work as normal; each action adds a state.
4. Click an earlier state to roll the image back, or click the snapshot to return to it.
5. To undo only part of a change, click the source box beside the snapshot and paint with the History Brush (Y).
tools.notes: History is not saved with the file - it is lost when the document closes. Deleting a state also deletes everything after it. Very high History States counts can exhaust the scratch disk on large documents.

tools.name: Actions
tools.description: Records a sequence of Photoshop commands and replays it on demand, which is how repetitive production work - resize, sharpen, watermark, export - gets automated without scripting. Actions are grouped into sets saved as .atn files that can be shared between machines. Combined with File > Automate > Batch or a droplet, one action can be run over a whole folder of images. Modal steps can be paused so the operator enters a value, and any step can be toggled off without deleting it.
tools.usage: Window > Actions, or Alt+F9 (Windows). The panel menu offers Button Mode, Load Actions..., Save Actions... and Playback Options; File > Automate > Batch... runs an action across a folder, and File > Automate > Create Droplet... turns it into a drag-and-drop executable.

parameters.name: Record / Stop
parameters.description: Buttons at the bottom of the panel; everything you do between them is recorded into the selected action.

parameters.name: Toggle dialog on/off
parameters.description: Second column beside a step; when on, playback pauses at that step so the user can change the settings.

parameters.name: Toggle item on/off
parameters.description: First column checkbox; skips a step during playback without deleting it.

parameters.name: Insert Menu Item / Insert Stop
parameters.description: Panel-menu commands for recording steps Photoshop cannot capture directly, and for showing a message mid-action.

parameters.name: Playback Options
parameters.description: Accelerated, Step by Step, or a pause of N seconds between steps - use Step by Step to debug an action.

tools.notes: Not everything is recordable - brush strokes and some tool work are not. Use Insert Menu Item for commands that refuse to record. Actions that reference absolute file paths break on other machines unless Batch supplies the folders.

tools.name: Brushes
tools.description: Holds the brush presets - each one a tip plus its recorded size, hardness, dynamics and often colour and blend mode - organised into expandable groups. This is where you load third-party .abr brush sets, build your own groups, and pick a brush without leaving the canvas. It is the preset library; the behaviour of the selected brush is edited in the Brush Settings panel.
tools.usage: Window > Brushes. No default keyboard shortcut (F5 opens Brush Settings, not this panel). The same list appears in the Brush Preset picker at the left of the options bar when a painting tool is active, and by right-clicking on the canvas.

parameters.name: Groups
parameters.description: Folders of presets; drag brushes between them, and use the panel menu to rename or export a group.

parameters.name: Import Brushes...
parameters.description: Panel-menu command that loads an .abr brush set. Double-clicking an .abr file also loads it.

parameters.name: New Brush Preset
parameters.description: Saves the current tip and settings, with optional Capture Brush Size in Preset, Include Tool Settings and Include Colour.

parameters.name: Legacy Brushes
parameters.description: Panel menu > Legacy Brushes restores the pre-CC 2018 default brush sets.

tools.example:
1. Window > Brushes.
2. Panel menu > Import Brushes... and select a downloaded .abr file.
3. Expand the new group and click a brush to load it.
4. Adjust size with [ and ], hardness with Shift+[ and Shift+].
5. Panel menu > New Brush Preset... to save your tweaked version, ticking Capture Brush Size in Preset.

tools.name: Brush Settings
tools.description: The engine room of the brush: tip shape, spacing, and the dynamics sections - Shape Dynamics, Scattering, Texture, Dual Brush, Colour Dynamics, Transfer, Brush Pose - plus the toggles for Noise, Wet Edges, Build-up, Smoothing and Protect Texture. Every parameter can be driven by pen pressure, tilt, stylus wheel or rotation, which is how a flat tip becomes a responsive natural-media brush. A live preview strip at the bottom shows the resulting stroke. Use it whenever a stock brush is nearly right but needs different jitter, spacing or pressure response.
tools.usage: Window > Brush Settings, or press F5. Also reachable from the folder icon at the right of the options bar when a painting tool is active.

parameters.name: Brush Tip Shape
parameters.description: Size, Angle, Roundness, Hardness and Spacing. Spacing below about 10% gives a continuous stroke; high values give a dotted trail.

parameters.name: Shape Dynamics
parameters.description: Size, Angle and Roundness Jitter with Control set to Off, Fade, Pen Pressure, Pen Tilt or Stylus Wheel.

parameters.name: Scattering
parameters.description: Spreads brush marks off the stroke path, with Count and Count Jitter.

parameters.name: Transfer
parameters.description: Opacity and Flow jitter - the section that makes a brush respond to pen pressure for build-up painting.

parameters.name: Smoothing
parameters.description: Stroke smoothing for steadier lines; also exposed as a percentage in the options bar.

tools.example:
1. Press B for the Brush tool, then F5 for Brush Settings.
2. Click Brush Tip Shape and set Spacing to 1% for a smooth stroke.
3. Tick Shape Dynamics and set Size Jitter Control to Pen Pressure.
4. Tick Transfer and set Opacity Jitter Control to Pen Pressure.
5. Watch the preview strip at the bottom, then save the result via the Brushes panel > New Brush Preset...

tools.name: Color
tools.description: Sets the foreground and background colours without opening the Colour Picker. The panel menu switches between sliders (RGB, HSB, CMYK, Lab, Greyscale, Web Colour) and the visual pickers - Hue Cube, Brightness Cube, Colour Wheel and the Colour Ramp strip along the bottom. The Colour Wheel view in particular makes it easy to pick harmonious complements by eye. Use it for continuous colour mixing while painting; use Swatches when you need exact, repeatable values.
tools.usage: Window > Color, or press F6. Click the foreground or background chip in the panel to make it active; clicking the already-active chip opens the full Colour Picker.

parameters.name: Slider set
parameters.description: Panel menu: RGB, HSB, CMYK, Lab, Greyscale or Web Colour sliders.

parameters.name: Hue Cube / Brightness Cube / Colour Wheel
parameters.description: Panel-menu visual picker modes.

parameters.name: Colour Ramp
parameters.description: The strip at the bottom; panel menu > Colour Ramp changes it between RGB, CMYK, Greyscale and Current Colours spectra.

parameters.name: Out-of-gamut warning
parameters.description: Small triangle icon shown when the chosen colour cannot be printed in the current CMYK working space; click it to snap to the nearest printable colour.

tools.example:
1. Press F6 to open the Color panel.
2. Panel menu > Colour Wheel.
3. Click the foreground chip to make it active.
4. Drag on the wheel for hue and on the triangle for saturation and brightness.
5. Press X at any time to swap foreground and background, or D to reset them to black and white.

tools.name: Swatches
tools.description: Stores named colours in groups so a project's palette stays consistent and reusable. Photoshop ships with themed groups (Pastels, Light, Dark, Greys and more) and you can add the current foreground colour with one click, import .aco and .ase swatch files, or pull a palette straight from a Creative Cloud Library. Use it whenever the same colours must be applied repeatedly across a document or a set of documents.
tools.usage: Window > Swatches. No default keyboard shortcut. Click a swatch to set the foreground colour; Ctrl+click sets the background colour. The plus icon at the bottom adds the current foreground colour as a new swatch.

parameters.name: Groups
parameters.description: Folders of swatches; create one from the panel menu > New Swatch Group... and drag swatches into it.

parameters.name: Import Swatches...
parameters.description: Panel-menu command that loads .aco (Photoshop) or .ase (Creative Suite exchange) palettes shared from Illustrator or InDesign.

parameters.name: Export Swatches for Exchange...
parameters.description: Writes an .ase file the rest of Creative Cloud can read.

parameters.name: Legacy Swatches
parameters.description: Panel menu entry that restores the older default swatch sets.

tools.example:
1. Window > Swatches.
2. Panel menu > New Swatch Group... and name it after the project.
3. Set a foreground colour, then click the plus icon at the bottom of the panel and name the swatch.
4. Drag the new swatch into the project group.
5. Panel menu > Export Swatches for Exchange... to share the palette with Illustrator or InDesign.

tools.name: Gradients
tools.description: A preset library of gradients organised into groups (Basics, Blues, Purples, Pinks, Iridescents, Pastels, Photographic Toning and others). Clicking a preset while the Gradient tool is active loads it; dragging a preset onto a layer in the canvas or Layers panel creates a live, re-editable Gradient Fill layer instead of baking pixels in. Use it for backgrounds, sky replacements, duotones via Gradient Map, and UI design fills.
tools.usage: Window > Gradients. No default keyboard shortcut. Works with the Gradient tool (G) and with Layer > New Fill Layer > Gradient...; the same presets appear in the gradient picker in the options bar.

parameters.name: Groups
parameters.description: Folders of gradient presets; the panel menu adds, renames and exports them.

parameters.name: Drag to canvas
parameters.description: Dragging a preset onto the image creates a non-destructive Gradient Fill layer with its own mask.

parameters.name: New Gradient Preset
parameters.description: Saves the gradient currently loaded in the Gradient Editor into the panel.

parameters.name: Import Gradients...
parameters.description: Loads a .grd gradient set.

tools.example:
1. Window > Gradients.
2. Expand a group and drag a preset onto the image - a Gradient Fill layer is created.
3. Double-click the Gradient Fill layer thumbnail to change angle, scale and style.
4. Set the layer's blend mode to Soft Light for a toning effect.
5. To build your own, press G, click the gradient strip in the options bar to open the Gradient Editor, then save it back into the panel.

tools.name: Patterns
tools.description: Holds tiling pattern presets - trees, grass, water, paper and any you define yourself - in groups. Patterns are used by Edit > Fill > Pattern, the Pattern Overlay layer style, Pattern Fill layers, the Pattern Stamp tool and the Healing Brush in Pattern mode. Dragging a preset onto a layer creates a live Pattern Fill layer whose scale and angle stay editable. Define your own from any rectangular selection with Edit > Define Pattern.
tools.usage: Window > Patterns. No default keyboard shortcut. Create a pattern with Edit > Define Pattern... from a rectangular (unfeathered) selection; apply with Edit > Fill (Shift+F5) > Contents: Pattern, or Layer > New Fill Layer > Pattern...

parameters.name: Define Pattern
parameters.description: Edit > Define Pattern... turns the current rectangular selection, or the whole layer, into a new preset.

parameters.name: Drag to canvas
parameters.description: Creates a Pattern Fill layer with editable Scale, Angle and the Link with Layer option.

parameters.name: Import Patterns...
parameters.description: Loads a .pat pattern set.

parameters.name: Legacy Patterns and More
parameters.description: Panel-menu entry restoring the older default pattern libraries.

tools.example:
1. Make a rectangular selection of a seamless tile with the Rectangular Marquee tool (M) - feather must be 0.
2. Edit > Define Pattern..., name it, click OK.
3. Window > Patterns to confirm it appears in the list.
4. Drag it onto a layer to create a Pattern Fill layer.
5. Double-click the fill layer thumbnail to change Scale and Angle at any time.

tools.name: Styles
tools.description: Stores complete layer-style recipes - drop shadows, bevels, strokes, overlays, glows - as one-click presets grouped by theme (Basics, Natural, Fur, Fabric, Photographic Effects and so on). Clicking a style applies the whole stack to the active layer, where it remains live and editable in the Layer Style dialog. This is the fastest way to make text and shape layers consistent across a design, and to reuse an effect you have spent time tuning.
tools.usage: Window > Styles. No default keyboard shortcut. Click a preset to apply it to the active layer, or drag it onto a layer in the canvas or Layers panel. Save the current layer's effects as a new style with the plus icon at the bottom of the panel, or the New Style... button in the Layer Style dialog (Layer > Layer Style > Blending Options..., or double-click the layer).

parameters.name: Groups
parameters.description: Folders of style presets; manage them from the panel menu.

parameters.name: New Style
parameters.description: Captures the active layer's effects, and optionally its blending options, as a reusable preset.

parameters.name: Import Styles...
parameters.description: Loads an .asl style library.

parameters.name: Clear Style
parameters.description: Panel icon that strips all effects from the active layer.

tools.example:
1. Select a text layer.
2. Window > Styles and click a preset - the whole effect stack is applied.
3. Double-click the layer in the Layers panel to open Layer Style and fine-tune the stroke and shadow.
4. Click New Style... in that dialog to save your version back to the panel.
5. Right-click the layer > Copy Layer Style, then right-click another layer > Paste Layer Style to reuse it directly.

tools.name: Shapes
tools.description: A library of vector custom shapes - arrows, banners, leaves, flowers, symbols, wild animals and so on - grouped into folders. Drag one onto the canvas, or select it in the Custom Shape tool's picker, to create a resolution-independent shape layer with editable fill, stroke and corner radius. Use it for iconography, decorative elements and quick vector masks. Your own paths can be added to the library with Edit > Define Custom Shape.
tools.usage: Window > Shapes. No default keyboard shortcut. Works with the Custom Shape tool (press U repeatedly to cycle to it); drag a preset from the panel straight onto the canvas to place it. Add your own with Edit > Define Custom Shape... while a path is selected.

parameters.name: Groups
parameters.description: Folders of shape presets; the panel menu adds, renames and exports them.

parameters.name: Drag to canvas
parameters.description: Places the shape as a new shape layer; hold Shift while dragging a handle to preserve proportions.

parameters.name: Import Shapes...
parameters.description: Loads a .csh custom shape set.

parameters.name: Legacy Shapes and More
parameters.description: Panel-menu entry that restores the pre-2020 default shape libraries.

tools.example:
1. Window > Shapes.
2. Expand a group and drag a shape onto the canvas - a shape layer is created.
3. Hold Shift while dragging a corner handle to scale it proportionally.
4. With the shape layer active, set Fill and Stroke in the options bar.
5. To add your own, draw a path with the Pen tool (P) and choose Edit > Define Custom Shape...

tools.name: Navigator
tools.description: Shows a thumbnail of the whole document with a red proxy rectangle marking the part currently visible in the document window, plus a zoom slider and a percentage field. Dragging the red box scrolls the view instantly, which is far quicker than scroll bars when you are zoomed in to 300% retouching a face and need to jump to another part of the image. Use it during any detailed zoomed-in work on a large document.
tools.usage: Window > Navigator. No default keyboard shortcut. Keyboard alternatives for the same job: Ctrl+plus and Ctrl+minus to zoom, Ctrl+0 to fit on screen, Ctrl+1 for 100%, and holding the spacebar for the Hand tool.

parameters.name: Proxy view area (red box)
parameters.description: Drag it to scroll; Ctrl+drag inside the thumbnail to draw a new zoom rectangle.

parameters.name: Zoom slider and percentage field
parameters.description: Set an exact zoom level; type a value and press Enter.

parameters.name: Panel Options
parameters.description: Panel menu > Panel Options changes the proxy rectangle colour when red is hard to see against the image.

tools.example:
1. Window > Navigator.
2. Drag the panel larger by its corner so the thumbnail is usable.
3. Type 300 in the zoom field and press Enter.
4. Drag the red box over the area you want to retouch.
5. Ctrl+drag a rectangle inside the thumbnail to zoom directly to that region.

tools.name: Info
tools.description: A live numeric readout of colour values under the pointer, cursor coordinates, and the dimensions of the current selection or transform. Because it can show two colour readouts at once - typically RGB and CMYK - it is the standard tool for checking that a highlight is not clipped or that a skin tone is neutral before print. It also reports document status, tool hints and the values of up to four colour sampler points placed with the Colour Sampler tool.
tools.usage: Window > Info, or press F8. Configure what it shows with the panel menu > Panel Options..., or by clicking the eyedropper icons inside the panel.

parameters.name: First / Second Colour Readout
parameters.description: Panel Options settings; a common pairing is Actual Colour plus CMYK Colour to spot out-of-gamut values.

parameters.name: Mouse Coordinates
parameters.description: Ruler units for the pointer position; change the unit in Panel Options or by right-clicking a ruler.

parameters.name: Colour samplers
parameters.description: Up to four fixed sample points placed with the Colour Sampler tool (in the Eyedropper group, I); their values are listed permanently in the panel.

parameters.name: Status Information
parameters.description: Panel Options checkboxes for document size, profile, dimensions, scratch sizes, efficiency, timing and current tool.

tools.example:
1. Press F8 to open the Info panel.
2. Panel menu > Panel Options... and set the Second Colour Readout to CMYK Colour.
3. Pick the Colour Sampler tool (nested with the Eyedropper, I) and click a highlight and a shadow.
4. Watch the sampler values while adjusting a Curves layer.
5. Exclamation marks beside CMYK values mean the colour is out of gamut for the current print profile.

tools.name: Histogram
tools.description: Graphs the tonal distribution of the image - shadows on the left, highlights on the right - so you can see clipping, low contrast and colour casts that the eye misses on an uncalibrated monitor. The All Channels View shows Red, Green and Blue separately, which is how colour casts are diagnosed. It updates live while you drag an adjustment, and the cached-data warning triangle tells you the graph was drawn from a low-resolution cache rather than the real pixels.
tools.usage: Window > Histogram. No default keyboard shortcut. The panel menu switches between Compact View, Expanded View and All Channels View, and offers Show Statistics and Uncached Refresh.

parameters.name: Channel
parameters.description: Dropdown in Expanded View: RGB composite, individual channels, Luminosity, or Colours (overlaid).

parameters.name: All Channels View
parameters.description: Draws a separate histogram per channel - the fastest way to spot a colour cast.

parameters.name: Uncached Refresh
parameters.description: Redraws the graph from the full-resolution image; also triggered by clicking the warning triangle.

parameters.name: Show Statistics
parameters.description: Adds Mean, Standard Deviation, Median, Pixels and the level under the pointer beneath the graph.

tools.example:
1. Window > Histogram.
2. Panel menu > Expanded View, then tick Show Statistics.
3. Click the warning triangle to force an uncached refresh from real pixel data.
4. Add a Levels adjustment layer and watch the graph update as you drag the black and white points.
5. Switch to All Channels View to check whether one channel is clipping before the others.

tools.name: Libraries
tools.description: Gives access to Creative Cloud Libraries - shared collections of colours, character and paragraph styles, layer styles, graphics, brushes, text and Adobe Stock assets that sync across Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign, XD and the mobile apps. Placing a graphic from a library creates a linked Smart Object, so updating the library asset updates every document that uses it. Use it to keep brand assets consistent across a team and across applications.
tools.usage: Window > Libraries. No default keyboard shortcut. Drag assets from the panel onto the canvas to place them; use the icons at the bottom of the panel to add the current foreground colour, layer style, character style or selected layers to the active library.

parameters.name: Library dropdown
parameters.description: Switches between your libraries and those shared with you; Create New Library... starts a new one.

parameters.name: Add elements
parameters.description: Buttons at the foot of the panel for adding the current colour, gradient, character style, layer style, text or selected layers.

parameters.name: Place linked / Place copy
parameters.description: Right-click a graphic: Place Linked keeps it tied to the library so edits propagate; Place Copy embeds an independent copy.

parameters.name: Collaborate / Share Link
parameters.description: Panel menu options to invite editors or publish a read-only link to a library.

parameters.name: Adobe Stock
parameters.description: Search field at the top of the panel licenses and saves Stock assets straight into the library.

tools.example:
1. Window > Libraries and choose Create New Library... from the dropdown.
2. Set a brand colour as the foreground and click the colour icon at the bottom of the panel to add it.
3. Select a logo layer group and click the graphic icon to add it to the library.
4. In another document, drag the logo from the panel onto the canvas - it arrives as a linked Smart Object.
5. Panel menu > Collaborate... to invite the rest of the team.
tools.notes: Linked library assets need the library to be available; a document sent to someone outside the library breaks the link unless you use File > Package or embed the Smart Object first.

tools.name: Comments & Version History panels
tools.description: Two collaboration panels that work with Photoshop's sharing features. The Comments panel collects feedback left by reviewers on a Share for review link, including pinned comments anchored to a point on the canvas, and lets you reply without leaving Photoshop. The Version History panel lists the automatically saved versions of a cloud document, lets you name and mark versions so they are retained, and restores any of them with Revert to this version. Use Comments to run client review inside the app, and Version History as a safety net that survives closing the file - unlike the History panel, which is session-only.
tools.usage: Window > Comments and Window > Version History. Neither has a default keyboard shortcut. Comments requires a review link created with Share > Share for review; Version History requires the file to be saved as a cloud document (File > Save As with Save to cloud documents, or File > Invite to Edit).

parameters.name: Share for review
parameters.description: Share > Share for review creates the web link reviewers comment on; choose Anyone with the link can comment or Invited only can comment.

parameters.name: Pinned comments
parameters.description: Comments anchored to a point on the canvas; clicking one in the panel jumps to that spot.

parameters.name: Reply / Resolve
parameters.description: Per-comment controls in the Comments panel.

parameters.name: Mark version
parameters.description: Version History control that retains a version permanently - unmarked versions are purged periodically.

parameters.name: Revert to this version
parameters.description: Moves the chosen version to the top of the stack so you can keep working from it.

tools.example:
1. Save the file as a cloud document so versions are tracked.
2. Choose Share > Share for review and copy the link to the reviewers.
3. Open Window > Comments to read and reply to the feedback as it arrives.
4. Open Window > Version History, hover a version and use the ellipsis to name and mark it before a big change.
5. If the change goes wrong, use Revert to this version in the same panel.
tools.notes: Version History only exists for cloud documents - a PSD stored on a local or network drive has no version stack. Refresh the review link after major edits so reviewers see the current artwork. The Character panel (Window > Character) is a separate typography panel and is unrelated to these two.

tools.name: Workspaces (Window > Workspace)
tools.description: Saves and restores complete panel layouts, and optionally the keyboard shortcuts, menus and toolbar that go with them. Photoshop ships with task-focused presets - Essentials, Photography, Painting, Graphic and Web, Motion - and you can save your own after arranging the panels you actually use. Because a workspace can carry a custom toolbar and a custom set of visible menu items, it is also the mechanism for simplifying Photoshop for a specific job or for a less experienced operator. Reset <name> restores a preset that has drifted out of shape.
tools.usage: Window > Workspace > Essentials (Default) / Graphic and Web / Motion / Painting / Photography, or New Workspace..., Delete Workspace..., Reset <name>, Keyboard Shortcuts & Menus... and Lock Workspace. The same list appears in the workspace switcher at the top right of the application bar. Edit > Toolbar... customises the toolbar; Edit > Keyboard Shortcuts (Alt+Shift+Ctrl+K) and Edit > Menus (Alt+Shift+Ctrl+M) open the same dialog used by New Workspace.

parameters.name: New Workspace...
parameters.description: Saves the current panel arrangement, with optional checkboxes to include Keyboard Shortcuts, Menus and Toolbar.

parameters.name: Reset <name>
parameters.description: Returns the current workspace to its saved state - the fix for panels that have been dragged somewhere unusable.

parameters.name: Lock Workspace
parameters.description: Prevents panels being dragged out of place accidentally, useful on a pen display.

parameters.name: Keyboard Shortcuts & Menus...
parameters.description: Opens the dialog where shortcuts and menu visibility are edited before saving them into a workspace.

tools.example:
1. Close the panels you never use and open the ones you do (for example Window > Histogram, Window > Info, Window > Actions).
2. Drag them into the dock on the right and collapse them to icons.
3. Window > Workspace > New Workspace...
4. Name it 'Retouching' and tick Keyboard Shortcuts, Menus and Toolbar.
5. Click Save. If the layout ever breaks, Window > Workspace > Reset Retouching restores it.
tools.notes: The available presets change between releases - the 3D workspace disappeared once 3D features were removed - so check the menu rather than assuming a preset exists. Deleting a workspace also deletes its saved shortcut and menu sets.

tools.name: Adobe Camera Raw
tools.description: The raw processing engine shared by Photoshop, Bridge and Lightroom. Camera raw files opened in Photoshop pass through its dialog automatically, where exposure, white balance, lens corrections, geometry, colour grading, noise reduction and local masks are applied to the raw data before any pixels are rendered. The same engine is available as Filter > Camera Raw Filter on an already-open layer, which brings the raw controls - including AI Select Subject, Select Sky and Select Objects masking - to JPEGs, TIFFs and composites. Run it on a Smart Object to keep the settings re-editable.
tools.usage: Filter > Camera Raw Filter... (Shift+Ctrl+A) for an open layer. Raw files opened with File > Open (Ctrl+O) launch the dialog automatically; File > Open As... forces a specific format. Preferences at Edit > Preferences > Camera Raw... In the dialog, hold Shift so Open Image becomes Open Object to bring the file in as a Smart Object.

parameters.name: Edit panel
parameters.description: Basic, Curve, Detail, Colour Mixer, Colour Grading, Optics, Geometry, Effects and Calibration sections.

parameters.name: Masking
parameters.description: Local adjustments with Select Subject, Select Sky, Select Objects, Select People, Brush, Linear and Radial Gradient, plus Colour and Luminance range refinements.

parameters.name: Presets and Snapshots
parameters.description: Saved looks and saved states of the current edit, shared with Lightroom.

parameters.name: Open Object
parameters.description: Shift-click Open Image (or set Workflow Options > Open in Photoshop as Smart Objects) so the Camera Raw settings stay editable after the file reaches Photoshop.

parameters.name: Workflow Options
parameters.description: Link at the bottom of the dialog that sets colour space, bit depth, output size and sharpening for the rendered file.

tools.example:
1. Select the layer to process and convert it with Filter > Convert for Smart Filters.
2. Press Shift+Ctrl+A to open the Camera Raw Filter.
3. Set white balance and exposure in Basic, then fix distortion in Optics and Geometry.
4. Use Masking > Select Sky to darken only the sky.
5. Click OK. Because the layer is a Smart Object, double-clicking the Camera Raw Filter entry in the Layers panel reopens the dialog with every slider intact.
tools.notes: Applied to an ordinary pixel layer the filter is destructive - always convert to a Smart Object first. Camera Raw must be up to date to read files from newly released cameras; update it through the Creative Cloud desktop app.

tools.name: Adobe Bridge
tools.description: A separate Creative Cloud application that browses, previews, rates, keywords and batch-processes files, and acts as the front end for Photoshop's automation commands. It reads camera raw files, PSDs, PDFs, InDesign documents and video without opening the host application, and shows full metadata including EXIF and IPTC. Use it to cull a shoot, apply Camera Raw settings to many files at once, or launch Photomerge, Merge to HDR Pro, Batch, Image Processor and Load Files into Photoshop Layers on a selected group of images. Bridge is installed separately from the Creative Cloud desktop app.
tools.usage: File > Browse in Bridge... (Alt+Ctrl+O) from Photoshop. From inside Bridge, select files and use Tools > Photoshop > Batch..., Image Processor..., Merge to HDR Pro, Photomerge or Load Files into Photoshop Layers; Stacks > Auto-Stack Panorama/HDR groups bracketed and overlapping shots automatically.

parameters.name: Tools > Photoshop
parameters.description: Submenu that hands the selected files to Photoshop's automation commands.

parameters.name: Stacks > Auto-Stack Panorama/HDR
parameters.description: Groups images into stacks by capture time, exposure and alignment ready for merging - timestamps must be within about 18 seconds.

parameters.name: Labels and ratings
parameters.description: Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+5 set star ratings; Ctrl+6 to Ctrl+9 set colour labels. Used with the Filter panel to cull a shoot.

parameters.name: Metadata and Keywords panels
parameters.description: Edit IPTC, copyright and keywords across many selected files at once.

parameters.name: Output workspace
parameters.description: Builds contact sheets and PDF presentations from the selected files.

tools.example:
1. In Photoshop choose File > Browse in Bridge... (Alt+Ctrl+O).
2. Navigate to the shoot folder and press Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+5 to rate the frames.
3. Use the Filter panel to show only the four- and five-star images.
4. Select the bracketed set and choose Tools > Photoshop > Merge to HDR Pro.
5. Or select a whole folder and choose Tools > Photoshop > Image Processor... to convert everything to sized JPEGs.
tools.notes: Bridge is not installed with Photoshop by default - install it from the Creative Cloud desktop app or File > Browse in Bridge will simply fail. The Mini Bridge panel of older versions no longer exists.

tools.name: Photomerge & Merge to HDR Pro
tools.description: Two stitching commands under File > Automate. Photomerge aligns and blends a series of overlapping photographs into a single panorama, offering Auto, Perspective, Cylindrical, Spherical, Collage and Reposition layouts plus vignette removal, geometric distortion correction and content-aware filling of the transparent edges. Merge to HDR Pro combines several exposures of the same scene into one high dynamic range image and then tone-maps it down to 16- or 8-bit for normal editing, with Local Adaptation controls for detail, glow and tone curve. Use Photomerge for wide scenes that will not fit one frame, and Merge to HDR Pro for high-contrast interiors and backlit landscapes.
tools.usage: File > Automate > Photomerge... and File > Automate > Merge to HDR Pro... Neither has a default keyboard shortcut. Both can also be launched from Adobe Bridge with the source files selected, via Tools > Photoshop > Photomerge or Tools > Photoshop > Merge to HDR Pro.

parameters.name: Layout (Photomerge)
parameters.description: Auto, Perspective (centre frame is the reference), Cylindrical (reduces bow-tie distortion in wide panoramas), Spherical (for 360-degree sets), Collage (aligns without stretching) and Reposition (aligns by overlap only).

parameters.name: Blend Images Together
parameters.description: Photomerge option that smooths the seams between frames.

parameters.name: Vignette Removal / Geometric Distortion Correction
parameters.description: Photomerge options that compensate for darkened corners and lens distortion before blending.

parameters.name: Content Aware Fill Transparent Areas
parameters.description: Photomerge option that fills the ragged transparent border created by alignment, saving a manual crop.

parameters.name: Mode (Merge to HDR Pro)
parameters.description: Output bit depth: 32 Bit keeps all the HDR data, 16 Bit and 8 Bit tone-map it immediately with Local Adaptation.

parameters.name: Remove ghosts
parameters.description: Merge to HDR Pro option that picks one source frame for moving subjects so people and leaves do not smear.

tools.example:
1. File > Automate > Photomerge...
2. Choose Files or Folder under Use, then Browse (or Add Open Files) to load the overlapping frames.
3. Pick a Layout - Auto for most sets, Cylindrical for very wide ones.
4. Tick Blend Images Together, Vignette Removal and Content Aware Fill Transparent Areas, then click OK.
5. For a bracketed set instead, use File > Automate > Merge to HDR Pro..., set Mode to 16 Bit with Local Adaptation, tick Remove ghosts and adjust the tone curve.
tools.notes: Photomerge produces a multi-layer document with masks; flatten it before cropping. Merge to HDR Pro needs exposure metadata - if it is missing, Photoshop asks for EV values in the Manually Set EV dialog. Shoot on a tripod with fixed white balance and aperture for the cleanest results in both.

tools.name: Artboards
tools.description: Lets one Photoshop document hold several independent canvases side by side, each with its own size, background and layer group. They are the standard way to design a set of screens, ad sizes or social formats together so shared elements stay consistent, and they export cleanly one file per artboard. Each artboard appears in the Layers panel as a special group, and layers dragged onto an artboard are clipped to it automatically. The Artboard tool is nested with the Move tool.
tools.usage: File > New (Ctrl+N) with the Artboards checkbox ticked, or Layer > New > Artboard... in an existing document, or the Artboard tool nested with the Move tool (V) - drag to create one, or use Add New Artboard in its options bar. Layers panel menu > Artboard from Layers converts selected layers into an artboard; Layer > Duplicate Artboard copies one. Export with File > Export > Artboards to Files... or File > Export > Artboards to PDF...

parameters.name: Artboards checkbox (New Document)
parameters.description: Turns a new document into an artboard document; presets such as Mobile, Web and Art & Illustration supply standard sizes.

parameters.name: Artboard tool
parameters.description: Nested with the Move tool; drag to draw a new artboard, or click the plus handles beside an existing one to add a sibling.

parameters.name: Add New Artboard (options bar)
parameters.description: Choose a size preset from the list, then click in the document to place it.

parameters.name: Layer > Duplicate Artboard
parameters.description: Copies an artboard and all its contents, the fast way to create a variant.

parameters.name: Artboards to Files / Artboards to PDF
parameters.description: File > Export commands that write one image per artboard, or a single multi-page PDF.

tools.example:
1. File > New (Ctrl+N), tick Artboards, choose the Mobile preset, click Create.
2. Select the Artboard tool (nested with the Move tool) and click a plus handle to add a second artboard.
3. Design on the first artboard; drag a layer onto the second and it is clipped to that artboard.
4. Select the artboard group in the Layers panel and choose Layer > Duplicate Artboard to make a variant.
5. File > Export > Artboards to Files... to write one PNG per artboard.
tools.notes: Artboard documents can grow large and some filters and automation behave differently inside them. A layer dragged partly off an artboard is clipped visually but still exists - check before exporting.

tools.name: Export As / Save for Web (Legacy) / Quick Export
tools.description: Photoshop's three routes to a web- or screen-ready file, all under File > Export and all leaving the PSD untouched. Export As is the modern dialog: PNG, JPG, GIF, SVG and WebP, multiple scale factors (1x, 2x, 3x) in one pass, per-asset canvas size and sRGB conversion. Save for Web (Legacy) is the older dialog kept for its side-by-side quality comparison, precise file-size targeting, GIF colour-table control and animation preview. Quick Export as PNG writes a file in one click using the format and location set in Preferences, which is the right choice when you are exporting the same asset repeatedly during iteration.
tools.usage: File > Export > Export As... (Alt+Shift+Ctrl+W), File > Export > Save for Web (Legacy)... (Alt+Shift+Ctrl+S), File > Export > Quick Export as PNG (no default shortcut, and the format is configurable). Right-clicking a layer, group or artboard in the Layers panel offers Export As... and Quick Export As for just that item. Defaults live in File > Export > Export Preferences... (Edit > Preferences > Export). Related: File > Export > Layers to Files... and File > Export > Artboards to Files...

parameters.name: Format
parameters.description: Export As: PNG, JPG, GIF, SVG, WebP. Save for Web: JPEG, PNG-8, PNG-24, GIF, WBMP.

parameters.name: Scale All Sizes
parameters.description: Export As control that writes 1x, 2x and 3x versions with suffixes in a single operation.

parameters.name: Convert to sRGB
parameters.description: Export As and Save for Web option that makes colour predictable in browsers; leave it on for web work.

parameters.name: Quick Export format and location
parameters.description: Set in Preferences > Export: the file type, and whether to ask each time or drop assets into an adjacent folder.

parameters.name: Metadata
parameters.description: Export As lets you keep Copyright and Contact Info; Save for Web strips most metadata by default, which is why its files are smaller.

tools.notes: Save for Web is legacy and does not support newer formats such as WebP or SVG; Export As does not offer its 4-up quality comparison or GIF colour-table editing, so both remain useful. Neither command changes the PSD - use File > Save As for that. An Export preference exists to restore the older Export As interface if you prefer it.

tools.name: Print (File > Print) & colour management
tools.description: Opens the Photoshop Print Settings dialog, which handles printer and paper selection, position and scale, output marks, and - most importantly - who converts the colour. Under Color Management you choose either Photoshop Manages Colors, supplying a printer/ink/paper profile and a rendering intent, or Printer Manages Colors, leaving the conversion to the driver; picking both, or neither, is the classic cause of colour casts. The surrounding commands - Edit > Color Settings, Convert to Profile, Assign Profile, and View > Proof Setup with Proof Colors - define the working spaces and let you soft-proof the print on screen before committing paper to it.
tools.usage: File > Print... (Ctrl+P) opens Photoshop Print Settings; File > Print One Copy (Alt+Shift+Ctrl+P) reprints with the last settings and no dialog. Supporting commands: Edit > Color Settings... (Shift+Ctrl+K), Edit > Convert to Profile..., Edit > Assign Profile..., View > Proof Setup > Custom..., View > Proof Colors (Ctrl+Y) and View > Gamut Warning (Shift+Ctrl+Y).

parameters.name: Color Handling
parameters.description: Photoshop Manages Colors (use with a custom printer/paper profile) or Printer Manages Colors (let the driver convert). Turn the other one off in the driver, or colours are converted twice.

parameters.name: Printer Profile
parameters.description: The ICC profile for the specific printer, ink and paper combination.

parameters.name: Rendering Intent
parameters.description: Perceptual, Saturation, Relative Colorimetric or Absolute Colorimetric - Relative Colorimetric with Black Point Compensation is the usual choice for photographs.

parameters.name: Normal Printing / Hard Proofing
parameters.description: Dropdown at the top of the Colour Management section; Hard Proofing simulates another output device on this printer.

parameters.name: Position and Size
parameters.description: Centre, scale to fit, and print resolution; Print Selected Area crops to the current selection.

parameters.name: Color Settings (Shift+Ctrl+K)
parameters.description: Sets the RGB and CMYK working spaces and the policies used when an opened file's embedded profile does not match.

tools.notes: Double colour management - Photoshop and the driver both converting - is the single most common printing fault; exactly one of them must be in charge. Soft-proofing only means anything on a calibrated, profiled monitor. Edit > Assign Profile reinterprets the existing numbers, while Edit > Convert to Profile changes the numbers to preserve the appearance; they are not interchangeable.
